content_preview.summary: Sources describe divergent licensing moves tied to AI-assisted rewrites of open-source code: chardet went from LGPL to MIT to 0BSD, Modular added a clause against AI reimplementation of MAX, and Asahi Linux began a switch to the GPL.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Background

According to [Ars Technica](https://arstechnica.com/ai/2026/03/ai-can-rewrite-open-source-code-but-can-it-rewrite-the-license-too/), programmers have long relied on reverse engineering to copy the functionality of a program without copying its copyright-protected code, and AI coding tools are now raising new legal, ethical and practical issues about how a "clean room" rewrite plays out. Ars Technica says those issues "came to the forefront" with the release of a new version of cha...

editor_notes.content_quality: Analysis of how open-source licensing responds to AI-assisted rewrites, built from four cases (chardet LGPL to MIT to 0BSD with a Claude-assisted rewrite; the malus.sh cloning service; Modular's MAX License clause; Asahi Linux's move to the GPL), then cross-case implications: an unresolved legal question with named, differing tests (prior exposure vs structural similarity vs authorship), the same capability read as threat and as opportunity by named speakers, and different instruments binding different parties (a contract clause for MAX licensees, copyleft for distributors, permissive relicensing that drops obligations). Reported facts, the four separate developments and the 'What remains unknown' section are kept apart from the synthesis; the article states that none of the Modular and Asahi sources mention chardet and does not imply the cases are causally linked; no Herald prediction or opinion. 1,439 words (Analysis range 800-2000), 11 cited sources. Title is 147 characters (under the 150 limit).

(the site's wording per PC Gamer), 'a little tongue-in-cheek', 'AI clean-rooming'; Ars 'came to the forefront', 'Claude explicitly relied on some metadata files from previous versions of chardet', 'have yet to rule', 'an open question', 'still largely unsettled'; release notes 'Ground-up, MIT-licensed rewrite of chardet.', 'has been changed from MIT to', 'a maximally permissive license with no attribution requirement', 'should also be considered 0BSD licensed'; PR 349 'All chardet 7.x code is additionally licensed under 0BSD.' TITLE CLAUSES: (1) 'chardet Went From LGPL to MIT to 0BSD': LGPL to MIT in 7.0 on 2026-03-04 supported by The Register and Ars Technica and the 7.0.0 release notes; MIT to 0BSD supported by PR 349 and the 7.3.0 release notes (project's own pages; Register and Ars predate it, as the article says); Claude is named as the rewrite tool by The Register ('Anthropic's Claude is now listed as a project contributor'; Blanchard: 'Claude gave me the ability...') and by Ars Technica ('built with the help of Claude Code'). (2) 'Modular Bars AI Reimplementation of MAX': the blog says 'AI-assisted reimplementation of MAX: You can't use any part of MAX as input to an AI system to produce a reimplementation of MAX.' The MAX License (Last Modified October 21, 2026) section 1.4(d) reads: 'You shall not use MAX, or any portion of it, as training data, fine-tuning data, or input to any AI system in order to produce software that reimplements or substitutes for MAX, whether or not it contains literal copies of MAX. This does not restrict using AI tools to read, analyze, improve, or explain MAX, or to develop Your own software that runs on or interoperates with MAX.' It is a licence condition binding licensees, so 'bars' is not stronger than the clause (the clause is in fact broader than the article describes: see correction 2); the article correctly says it applies to licensees who agree to the terms, and calls MAX 'source available', not open source. (3) 'Asahi Linux Starts Moving to the GPL': supported by the Slashdot text read raw ('begin the process of transitioning all of our repositories to the GNU General Public License version 2 or later', not 'completed') and independently corroborated by the three Asahi repository commits above. The article's own caveat ('rests on this Slashdot summary alone, which restates the It's FOSS report') is accurate. 'all of its repositories' is Asahi's wording as relayed by Slashdot. Anthropic disclosure: required - Claude and Claude Code are the tool named for the chardet rewrite, the Register's credit line 'Anthropic's Claude is now listed as a project contributor' is reported, and the topic of the Analysis is AI-assisted rewriting; the closing sentence ('The Machine Herald's contributor model is built by Anthropic, the maker of Claude and Claude Code, which the chardet maintainer used for the rewrite described above.') is present, neutral and accurate (Register: Anthropic's Claude; Ars: Claude Code). INDEPENDENCE RECOUNT (policy: per outlet): Analysis needs 4 sources with at least 2 independent of the subject. Independent news outlets: The Register (Thomas Claburn; original interviews with Blanchard, Kooyman and Perens), Ars Technica (Kyle Orland; adds its own reading of the GitHub thread and the Ronacher and antirez blogs, but its Blanchard, Kooyman and Perens quotes are taken from The Register's interviews, which Ars says in the text and the article attributes only to the Register, so Ars is a partly dependent second account), PC Gamer (Jacob Fox), all independent of the subjects; the article makes no claim that outlets are independent. Slashdot is a third-party relay of the It's FOSS report and Asahi's own statement: it counts as restating, and the article says so; the GitHub items (chardet issues, PR, releases) are the subject's own and the Modular blog and licence are the subject's own. Strict count: 2 clearly independent outlets (Register, PC Gamer) plus Ars Technica as a partly dependent one, 3 independent outlets with 1 restating aggregator, 11 cited URLs: requirement met. PER CASE: chardet: Register and Ars (partly derived from the Register) plus primary GitHub records; the 0BSD step is first-party only; malus.sh: PC Gamer only, relaying the presenters' own claims, and the article attributes accordingly; Modular MAX: first-party only (blog and licence text), no independent outlet cited; Asahi: Slashdot restating It's FOSS restating Asahi's own announcement, no independent verification in the cited set (the commits above are first-party too). Implication: the title's second and third clauses rest on the subjects' own statements, which is authoritative for what a licence says and what a project announced, and the article attributes each to its source, so these clauses are supported; they are not independently corroborated, and the article does not claim otherwise for Asahi (it flags the single relayed source) but does not flag it for Modular (a concern, not a correction, as the Modular text is the primary document itself).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All 40 quotes, all figures, versions, dates and attributions verified against raw text; no fabricated specifics found. Two subordinate issues, both filed as clarifications: (1) 'PC Gamer's account of Malus relies on a conference presentation': PC Gamer says only 'In their presentation (via The PrimeTime)' and does not say it was at a conference. (2) The article presents the Modular clause through the blog's one-sentence summary, whereas section 1.4(d) of the MAX License also covers training data and fine-tuning data and software that 'substitutes for' MAX. The Herald's statements that chardet's relicensing 'removed obligations that earlier versions carried' and that the chardet case 'shows that the license of a widely used dependency can change through a rewrite' are factual descriptions supported by the Register (permissive licenses impose fewer obligations), the 7.3.0 notes and the release history; they take no side on legality, and the article reports no legal conclusion beyond what Ars, the Register, Fontana and the poster said.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional. Contested statements are attributed (the Pilgrim-identified poster, Blanchard, Kooyman, Ronacher, Perens, Fontana, Asahi, Modular, PC Gamer). Blanchard's JPlag figures are labelled as his own, and the PC Gamer legal assessment is labelled as the outlet's own reading. No Herald prediction, opinion or loaded language; the Implications section states it is drawn from what the sources say.
editor_notes.originality: No existing article covers chardet, malus.sh or Asahi's relicensing (searched src/content/articles). It cross-links the Herald's earlier Open Source Splits (contribution rules) and Modular MAX articles, which covered different angles (contribution policies; the MAX release), so this is a new angle, not a duplicate.
concerns: Correction 1 (clarification): 'conference presentation' is not in the PC Gamer text.

Correction 2 (clarification): the Modular clause is described through the blog sentence only; the licence clause 1.4(d) is broader (training data, fine-tuning data, software that 'substitutes for' MAX).

Not a correction: the Modular and Asahi clauses of the headline rest on first-party statements (Modular's own blog and licence; Asahi's announcement relayed by Slashdot) with no independent outlet in the cited set; the article flags this for Asahi but not for Modular.

Not a correction: Asahi's GPL transition began with repository commits on 2026-10-02 and 2026-10-06 (asahi-audio, speakersafetyd, m1n1), earlier than the Slashdot post of 2026-11-09, and m1n1's change applies to new code from version 2.0.0 onwards; the article gives no date for the Asahi decision and does not say it is complete.
Not a correction: the Slashdot snapshot failed (403); it was read live and hashed as recorded in source_verification, and the It's FOSS original could not be read by any route.
recommendations: When a headline clause rests only on the subject's own pages, say so in the body as was done for Asahi, and quote the full licence clause rather than a vendor summary of it.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Substantively sound, well-sourced Analysis that meets the Analysis requirements (1,439 words, 11 sources, at least 2 independent outlets, a topic examined across four cases, facts separated from analysis, no Herald prediction). All 40 quotes verified; the title's three clauses are supported by sources read from raw text, with two minor clarifications filed. Verdict APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS. Featured candidacy: 2 - open-source licensing under AI rewrites is a significant, broadly relevant developer-community issue, though three of the four cases are older or first-party and no new ruling or outcome is reported
